server.title: NYC Charter, Administrative Code and Rules MCP server
server.description: An MCP server for searching and reading the New York City Charter, the Administrative Code and the Rules of the City of New York. It answers from an index BetaNYC builds from American Legal Publishing's bulk XML downloads, which ships with the package. It is for research only, not legal advice, and not the official text: check the code library before relying on any section.
keywords: rules of the city of new york

sources.title: New York City Charter
sources.what: The text of the New York City Charter, one record per section or chapter heading, with its citation and heading.
sources.source_name: New York City Charter, bulk XML download
sources.how_gathered: BetaNYC downloads the bulk XML file from American Legal Publishing's New York City code library, the site the NYC Law Department contracted for the Charter, Administrative Code and Rules, and builds an index from it. A scheduled job refreshes the index daily and publishes a new release when the text changed. The index ships with the npm package, so this server answers without going online.

changes.detail: The XML is split into one record per section or heading, with its citation pulled from the heading. BetaNYC also fixes text problems from the conversion: it decodes character codes the XML left as text (such as non-breaking spaces), removes American Legal Publishing's editing markers (such as [ALP S-054]) that leak into the body text, and puts back the space between a list number and the words after it. The Charter has no text in the old Symbol font, which the Administrative Code and the Rules use for some math signs and Greek letters, so no Charter character is changed for that. All line breaks are collapsed, so paragraphs and tables run together as one block of text. Deeper structure, such as which sections sit inside which title, is not kept.

known_gaps: Only the current text: no earlier versions of a section.
An XML file that cannot be read during the build is skipped, with a warning in the build log. get_version's section count shows if a document came up short.
Citations are worked out by BetaNYC from each heading, not given by the publisher, so they can be wrong or cut short. Check a citation against the heading and the official text.

terms.credit_line: Source: New York City Charter, American Legal Publishing code library for the City of New York.

caveats: Not legal advice. American Legal Publishing says its codes may not yet reflect the most current legislation, and may have temporary errors or omissions.
How current the text is: get_version gives the publisher's own 'current through' line. The date about_data reports is when BetaNYC built this server's index from the download.
The NYC Law Department says it contracted with American Legal Publishing Corporation for this site: https://www.nyc.gov/site/law/public-resources/laws-of-the-city-of-new-york.page
The publisher also takes error reports by phone, 800-445-5588, and the NYC Law Department takes them at NYCCodeRulesCharter@law.nyc.gov.

sources.title: New York City Administrative Code
sources.what: The text of the New York City Administrative Code, one record per section or chapter heading, and one for each appendix, reference standard or other part that holds text outside a section, with its citation and heading.
sources.source_name: New York City Administrative Code, bulk XML download
sources.how_gathered: BetaNYC downloads the bulk XML file from American Legal Publishing's New York City code library, the site the NYC Law Department contracted for the Charter, Administrative Code and Rules, and builds an index from it. A scheduled job refreshes the index daily and publishes a new release when the text changed. The index ships with the npm package, so this server answers without going online.

changes.detail: The XML is split into one record per section or chapter heading, and one for each part that holds text of its own outside a section, such as a Building Code reference standard (RS 18-1), an appendix, or an editor's note on a subchapter or article. Each record's citation is pulled from its heading. A reference standard keeps its own number (RS 18-1); any other part outside a section starts with the title and chapter it sits in (Title 20, Chapter 2, Subchapter 3). BetaNYC also fixes text problems from the conversion: it decodes character codes the XML left as text (such as non-breaking spaces), removes American Legal Publishing's editing markers (such as [ALP S-054]) that leak into the body text, and puts back the space between a list number and the words after it. Where the publisher's file sets a math sign or Greek letter in the old Symbol font, which shows them in place of ordinary characters, BetaNYC changes the ones it has checked to the character the font shows, using the Unicode Consortium's table for that font: ³ becomes ≥, £ becomes ≤ and D becomes Δ. Other characters set in that font, such as bullets and footnote marks, are left as the file has them. All line breaks are collapsed, so paragraphs and tables run together as one block of text. Each record in a numbered title also names that title, read from the XML, so a lettered title such as Title 16-A, which shares its parent's section numbers, is kept apart from Title 16. The local laws listed by year, which the publisher puts in no numbered title, name none. Deeper structure, such as the lettered and numbered subdivisions inside a section, is not kept.

known_gaps: Only the current text: no earlier versions of a section.
Pictures in the publisher's files are left out, because they have no text.
An XML file that cannot be read during the build is skipped, with a warning in the build log. get_version's section count shows if a document came up short.
Citations are worked out by BetaNYC from each heading, not given by the publisher, so they can be wrong or cut short. Check a citation against the heading and the official text.
A note the publisher puts on a whole title, such as an editor's note or an amendment line, is not in the index, because the index has no record for a title.

Characters set in the "WP Greek Helve" font are not changed yet, so they show as the ordinary letters the file holds. In the July 2026 files that is the Building Code's Table 1613.5 (§ BC 1613), whose over-strength factor Ω0 reads "S 0", and Administrative Code §§ 28-1001.2.1 and 28-1001.2.2, where ":mol/J" is μmol/J.

sources.title: Rules of the City of New York
sources.what: The text of the Rules of the City of New York, the rules City agencies adopt, one record per section or chapter heading, and one for each appendix, schedule or other part that holds text outside a section, with its citation and heading.
sources.source_name: Rules of the City of New York, bulk XML download
sources.how_gathered: BetaNYC downloads the bulk XML file from American Legal Publishing's New York City code library, the site the NYC Law Department contracted for the Charter, Administrative Code and Rules, and builds an index from it. A scheduled job refreshes the index daily and publishes a new release when the text changed. The index ships with the npm package, so this server answers without going online.

changes.detail: The XML is split into one record per section or chapter heading, and one for each part that holds text of its own outside a section, such as an appendix, a schedule of penalties, the Water Board's rate schedule, the Board of Health's resolutions, or a note on a subchapter. Each record's citation is pulled from its heading. A part outside a section starts with the title it sits in, and its chapter when it has one (Title 19, Chapter 55, Schedule A); a part of the Health Code starts with the code's name (New York City Health Code, Title IV, Part B, Article 175). BetaNYC also fixes text problems from the conversion: it decodes character codes the XML left as text (such as non-breaking spaces), removes American Legal Publishing's editing markers (such as [ALP S-054]) that leak into the body text, and puts back the space between a list number and the words after it. Where the publisher's file sets a math sign or Greek letter in the old Symbol font, which shows them in place of ordinary characters, BetaNYC changes the ones it has checked to the character the font shows, using the Unicode Consortium's table for that font: ³ becomes ≥, £ becomes ≤ and D becomes Δ. Other characters set in that font, such as bullets and footnote marks, are left as the file has them. All line breaks are collapsed, so paragraphs and tables run together as one block of text. Each record also names the title it sits in, so a rule can be cited as 15 RCNY § 1-01: each title of the Rules numbers its own sections. BetaNYC reads the title from the XML, and places the few chapters the XML does not put in a title, such as the Health Code and the Rent Guidelines Board's yearly orders, by the order of the publisher's records. Deeper structure, such as the lettered and numbered subdivisions inside a section, is not kept.

Pictures in the publisher's files are left out, because they have no text.
An XML file that cannot be read during the build is skipped, with a warning in the build log. get_version's section count shows if a document came up short.
Citations are worked out by BetaNYC from each heading, not given by the publisher, so they can be wrong or cut short. Check a citation against the heading and the official text.
A note the publisher puts on a whole title, such as an editor's note or an amendment line, is not in the index, because the index has no record for a title.

Characters set in the Wingdings font are not changed yet, so they show as the ordinary letters the file holds. In the July 2026 files that is the notice form in 28 RCNY § 25-101, whose check boxes read "o heat o hot water o cold water".
